title: Jyotiba Phule

cards.h: The first modern voice of the oppressed
cards.b: Jyotirao Govindrao Phule (1827-90) was a Maharashtra reformer who attacked caste as a system of Brahmin domination and built schools for girls and the lower castes. He is the start of the anti-caste tradition that runs to Periyar and Ambedkar, who called him one of his three gurus.

• 1848: first school for girls in Pune, with wife Savitribai.
  • 1863: home for widows' newborns (Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha).
  • 1873: Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth-Seekers' Society).
  • Works: Tritiya Ratna (1855), Gulamgiri (1873), Shetkaryacha Asud (1881), Sarvajanik Satyadharma (1891, posthumous).
  • 1888: given the title 'Mahatma' by a Bombay gathering.

Gulamgiri ('Slavery', 1873) is dedicated to Americans who ended slavery. Phule compares the plight of Shudras and Ati-Shudras to that of Black slaves.

His version of history: Aryan Brahmins invaded, defeated the native peoples, and made scriptures to justify slavery. The legendary king Bali stands for the original, just rule. The tale is a counter-history, not scholarship.

Phule rejected the Vedas, the varna theory and priestly rituals as inventions to keep power. He opposed idol worship, priest-mediated ceremonies, and promoted a universal, rational religion with one creator (Sarvajanik Satyadharma). Satyashodhak weddings were held without Brahmin priests.

He saw colonial rule as an opportunity but also criticised it.

He argued that lack of education is the root of Shudra misery: 'Without learning, intellect was lost; without intellect, morals; without morals, progress; without progress, wealth; without wealth, the Shudras were ruined.'

In Shetkaryacha Asud ('Cultivator's Whipcord', 1881) he showed how moneylenders, priests, and the colonial bureaucracy together exploited farmers. He told the Hunter Commission (1882) that the state spent too much on higher education for elites and too little on primary schooling.

Phule and Savitribai opened schools for girls from 1848, faced social boycott, and sheltered widows and illegitimate children. He urged widow remarriage and wrote of the need for women's education as the base of social change. He saw patriarchy and caste as linked systems.

• The Aryan-invasion theory is disputed by modern historians.
  • He mostly addressed Maratha-Kunbi and Mali communities, less the Dalits.
  • Brahmin leaders such as Tilak argued that social reform divided the nationalist front.
  • Positive: first to place social justice before political freedom.

Phule's Gulamgiri (1873) was dedicated to the American abolitionists, and critics note that his ideas of equality drew on Western liberal and Enlightenment thought.

Phule: social revolution first, anti-Brahmin. Ambedkar: constitutional and legal route, plus rights. Gandhi: reform within Hinduism through moral appeal. Ambedkar called Phule a guru together with Buddha and Kabir, and dedicated Who Were the Shudras? to him.

The Poona Pact of 1932, reached after Gandhi's fast against Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates, shows the gap between reform within Hinduism and a rights-based route.

Satyashodhak ideas shaped the non-Brahmin movement in Maharashtra, Periyar's Self-Respect Movement and Dalit-Bahujan politics. The Maharashtra and national debates on girls' education, reservation, and caste census all invoke him. Savitribai Phule is regarded as India's first woman teacher.

Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur reserved 50 per cent of government posts for non-Brahmins in 1902, a move in the same spirit as Phule's movement.

Structure: context, Satyashodhak Samaj, Gulamgiri thesis, education and peasants, women, critique, legacy.

Phule opened a girls' school in Bhide Wada, Pune, in 1848 with Savitribai Phule. The Satyashodhak Samaj, founded in 1873, held marriages without a priest.
